expectedConcepts: left join keeps all left rows

questionSnapshots.referenceAnswer: An inner join returns matched pairs; a left join also retains unmatched left rows and fills right columns with NULL. Filtering a right-table column in WHERE, instead of placing the condition in ON or accounting for NULL, removes those unmatched rows.

join order never matters

questions.answer: For the fictional placement tracker, the constraint was offline operation on one laptop with records surviving restarts. I chose SQLite transactions and parameterized queries. I considered JSON files, which are simple but require manual locking and recovery, and PostgreSQL, which supports many simultaneous users but requires a separate server. I tested rollback on invalid input, a unique constraint for duplicate applications, and quotes in user input to ensure parameters are treated as data.

questions.answer: In this fictional test project, a record appeared after saving but disappeared on restart. My first hypothesis was that the read query filtered it incorrectly. I reproduced the issue with a temporary database and inspected the row through a second connection before shutdown: the second connection could not see it. That evidence pointed to an uncommitted transaction rather than filtering. I traced the write path and found an early return before commit. I moved the transaction into a context manager that commits on success and rolls back on failure. A regression test inserts a record, closes the connection, reopens the database and asserts the same row exists; another test verifies failed validation leaves no partial row.

questions.question: Compare INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN. When can a LEFT JOIN unexpectedly reduce to inner-join behaviour?
questions.answer: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows. LEFT JOIN retains every left-side row, with NULL values for unmatched right-side columns. A WHERE condition on a right-side column such as WHERE jobs.status = active filters out those NULL-extended rows, effectively removing unmatched left rows and behaving like an inner join. If I want all applicants and only their active jobs, I put the status predicate in the ON clause: applicants LEFT JOIN jobs ON jobs.applicant_id = applicants.id AND jobs.status = the active parameter. I test applicants with zero jobs, only inactive jobs, and multiple active jobs; multiple matches correctly produce multiple rows.

questions.answer: First I measure the query on representative data and inspect EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for a full table scan or a temporary sort. For WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at, I would test a composite index on (user_id, created_at): equality on the leading column narrows the range and the second column provides ordered rows for that user. I compare the plan and latency before and after, including users with few and many rows and any LIMIT. I check existing indexes and avoid redundant ones. An index costs storage and slows inserts and updates, so I benchmark that too; stale statistics, selecting many columns, and low selectivity can affect whether the planner uses it.

conversation.text: For the fictional placement tracker, the constraint was offline operation on one laptop with records surviving restarts. I chose SQLite transactions and parameterized queries. I considered JSON files, which are simple but require manual locking and recovery, and PostgreSQL, which supports many simultaneous users but requires a separate server. SQLite fits single-user deployment; it is a trade-off because concurrent writers are limited. I verified persistence by inserting an application, restarting the process and reading it back. I tested rollback on invalid input, a unique constraint for duplicate applications, and quotes in user input to ensure parameters are treated as data.

conversation.text: In this fictional test project, a record appeared after saving but disappeared on restart. My first hypothesis was that the read query filtered it incorrectly. I reproduced the issue with a temporary database and inspected the row through a second connection before shutdown: the second connection could not see it. That evidence pointed to an uncommitted transaction rather than filtering. I traced the write path and found an early return before commit. I moved the transaction into a context manager that commits on success and rolls back on failure. A regression test inserts a record, closes the connection, reopens the database and asserts the same row exists; another test verifies failed validation leaves no partial row.

conversation.text: INNER JOIN returns only matching rows. LEFT JOIN retains every left-side row, with NULL values for unmatched right-side columns. A WHERE condition on a right-side column such as WHERE jobs.status = active filters out those NULL-extended rows, effectively removing unmatched left rows and behaving like an inner join. If I want all applicants and only their active jobs, I put the status predicate in the ON clause: applicants LEFT JOIN jobs ON jobs.applicant_id = applicants.id AND jobs.status = the active parameter. I test applicants with zero jobs, only inactive jobs, and multiple active jobs; multiple matches correctly produce multiple rows.

I compare the plan and latency before and after, including users with few and many rows and any LIMIT. I check existing indexes and avoid redundant ones. questionSnapshots.prompt: Explain the difference between mutable and immutable Python objects. Give one bug that shared mutable state can cause.
expectedConcepts: immutable values require a new object
aliasing or mutable defaults can share state
questionSnapshots.referenceAnswer: Lists and dictionaries can be changed in place, while values such as strings, tuples, and integers cannot. If two names reference one mutable object, a change through one name is visible through the other; a mutable default argument can therefore leak state across calls.
commonMisconceptions: const variables make Python objects immutable
tuples can never contain mutable members

criteria.label: Gives valid mutable and immutable examples

questionSnapshots.followUpCriteria: If the answer is strong, ask how copying differs from aliasing; if shared state is vague, request a concrete function example.
questionSnapshots.hint: Think about whether an operation changes an existing object identity or binds a name to a different object.

questionSnapshots.prompt: Compare INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN. When can a LEFT JOIN unexpectedly reduce to inner-join behaviour?
expectedConcepts: left join keeps all left rows
WHERE predicate on right table can remove null rows
questionSnapshots.referenceAnswer: An inner join returns matched pairs; a left join also retains unmatched left rows and fills right columns with NULL. Filtering a right-table column in WHERE, instead of placing the condition in ON or accounting for NULL, removes those unmatched rows.
commonMisconceptions: left join always returns more rows
join order never matters

criteria.label: Explains LEFT JOIN and NULL extension

questionSnapshots.followUpCriteria: Ask the student to place a status predicate correctly in ON versus WHERE.
questionSnapshots.hint: Trace what happens to an unmatched row after the join and then after WHERE.

questionSnapshots.prompt: A query filtering by user_id and sorting by created_at is slow. How would you investigate and choose an index?
questionSnapshots.referenceAnswer: Inspect the actual plan and row counts first. A composite index beginning with user_id and then created_at can support the equality filter and ordered retrieval. Validate selectivity and the plan, while accounting for additional write cost and storage.
commonMisconceptions: add separate indexes to every column
an index always makes every query faster
questionSnapshots.followUpCriteria: Ask why column order matters if the answer only says to add an index.
